verses.translation_literal: A prayer of an afflicted one, when he grows faint, and before YHWH he pours out his complaint.
verses.translation_dramatic: A prayer for one who is bowed down. When he is faint with grief, he does not hold his trouble in. Before the LORD he empties it out, every last word of his complaint.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the heading, and in the Hebrew it counts as verse 1, which is why the KJV numbers the psalm's first line 102:0 and then runs one verse behind. Do not play it as a title card. It tells the actor who is speaking: an 'ani, one who is bowed and poor, with nothing left to stand on. The verb yishpokh is 'pours out', the word used for water on the ground or blood from a vessel, and the KJV 'poureth out his complaint' keeps it. What the KJV hides is 'when he is overwhelmed'. The Hebrew ya'atof is to wrap, or to grow faint, as one folds up under a weight. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'those wrapped in hunger'; Radak sees a man who bends his body over himself in prayer. Play both: the fainting and the crouch. The word siach, 'complaint', is not a petition. It is a man talking his trouble through. The tradition hears the exiles in this voice (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri, Malbim), a whole people speaking as one afflicted man.

philological_notes.note: 'Afflicted, bowed down, poor.' It is the one pressed low by circumstance and without protector; here a person who has only God to speak to. Rashi hears Israel as an 'am 'ani, a poor people.

To wrap, cover; by extension to faint, to be enveloped by weakness (the same root as 'the faint with hunger' in Lam 2:19). Ibn Ezra compares 'those wrapped in hunger'; Radak and Meiri hear a man who folds himself up in prayer.
Not 'petition' but musing aloud, complaint, the telling of one's trouble. Metzudat Zion compares Job 7:11 'I will complain in the bitterness of my soul'.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, hear my prayer, and my cry for help, to you let it come.
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD, hear my prayer. Hear it. And my cry, the one that has no polish left in it, let it travel the whole way to you.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice begins with a bare imperative: shim'ah, 'hear!', with the extra syllable ah that makes it an urgent plea. Notice the word order in the second half: 'and my cry for help, TO YOU, let it come'. 'To you' is thrown forward, because the speaker has been crying to everyone and no one. In the ancient Near East a god who 'hears' acts; hearing is the first half of rescue. The KJV 'let my cry come unto thee' is faithful, but its smooth 'O LORD' loses the bare four-letter name that opens the line. The pair tefilah and shav'ah is a ladder: tefilah is a formal prayer, shav'ah the raw shout of someone in danger (Malbim: the prayer is for the whole people, the shav'ah is the cry for his own rescue). Ibn Ezra adds that God hears every prayer, so the point is that people should see that this one was heard.

philological_notes.note: A cry for help, the shout of the person in danger, more urgent than formal tefilah (prayer). Malbim distinguishes the two: prayer for the collective, cry for oneself.

verses.translation_literal: Do not hide your face from me on the day it is tight for me; incline to me your ear; on the day I call out, hurry, answer me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not turn your face away from me. Not today, not while the walls are closing in. Bend down your ear. On the day I call, do not make me wait: hurry, answer me.
verses.directors_commentary: Three requests and a rush. The face and the ear are the body of a king who sits on a throne; to 'hide the face' is to refuse an audience, and the exile feels God has turned his back (Radak links it to the curse of Deut 31:17, 'I will hide my face from them'). Ibn Ezra notes the paradox: a hidden face cannot see, but it may still hear, hence 'incline your ear'. The sense of tsar is 'narrow, tight', a day that squeezes, and the KJV 'in trouble' makes it sound like inconvenience. The repeated 'on the day' (beyom) gives the verse a drumbeat; the speaker counts days because he cannot count anything else. The last word run, maher 'anani, is two imperatives with no 'and': 'hurry, answer me'. No politeness, nothing between them. The KJV softens it with 'speedily', a word that belongs to a letter. This is a shout.

philological_notes.note: The verb 'to be narrow, tight', so a day when things close in. The KJV 'in trouble' loses the physical image of constriction.
'Incline your ear', a body image: the listener leans down. Ibn Ezra explains 'hide your face' as a parable: one who hides his face cannot see but can still hear.

verses.translation_literal: For my days have come to an end in smoke, and my bones like a hearth are burned.
verses.translation_dramatic: For my days are going up in smoke, thinning and drifting until they are gone. And my bones are dry and hot as the stones of a hearth where the fire has been burning all night.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the reason for the hurry, and it is fire. Time is consumed like fuel: yamai, 'my days', go up as smoke, and the Hebrew verb kalu means both 'finished' and 'consumed', so the days are used up the way wood is. The second line moves to the body. A mokad (here the short form ked) is the burning place, the altar-hearth of Lev 6:2, where the fire stays alight all night; Radak and Metzudat Zion both take it so, a place and not a log. That is why the KJV 'hearth' is right and ASV and YLT 'firebrand' are not. The verb nikharu is not 'burned' like a cooked meal but parched, scorched dry, as in Job 30:30 'my bones are parched with heat' (Rashi). Fever is the likely picture, which Meiri notes in his medical language. Actors should not play flames, but dryness: a man who is a dead branch near a fire.

philological_notes.note: A hearth, the burning place of an altar fire (Lev 6:2, mokdah). Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as the place where the fire burns; Ibn Ezra allows a two-word reading. KJV 'hearth' is right.
To be parched, scorched, dried; Rashi links it with Job 30:30 and Jer 6:29 (nachar mapuach, 'the bellows are scorched'). Not simply 'burned'.

token_glosses.gloss: they have come to an end

verses.translation_literal: It has been struck down like vegetation and has withered, my heart, for I have forgotten from eating my bread.
verses.translation_dramatic: My heart has been struck like the grass under a hard sun, and it has gone dry. I have even forgotten to eat my bread.
verses.directors_commentary: Sunstroke is the image, and the people who first heard it knew it well: in the Judean summer the east wind and the sun scorch the green in a day (compare Ps 37:2, 90:5-6). Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David both see grass struck by the sun; the heart is the grass. The verb hukkah is 'struck' as with a blow, and the KJV 'smitten' is right but archaic. The Hebrew word order puts 'my heart' last, after the verbs, as if the speaker can barely get to the thing that was struck. The ancient 'heart' is not the seat of feeling alone but of will and appetite, and that is why the loss of hunger follows at once: 'I have forgotten from eating my bread.' The KJV 'so that I forget to eat' makes this a result clause, but the Hebrew just says 'for'. Lechem is 'bread' and by extension the whole meal; it is the staple of the day, so to forget it is to forget how to live. Radak and Meiri explain the verse by the old medicine, where the heart's heat dries the body unless food moistens it; you need not play that, only the loss of appetite.

philological_notes.note: 'It has been struck down'; the word is spelled with vav and dagesh, an odd form noted by Radak and Meiri. The image is grass struck by the sun, not by a blow.
'I forgot away from eating', with privative min; a man so far gone that eating drops out of his mind. Not 'I forget to eat' as a result clause.

verses.translation_literal: From the sound of my groaning my bone clings to my flesh.
verses.translation_dramatic: From the sound of my own groaning, my bones cling to my flesh. There is nothing left between them.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the body shows what has been said. 'The sound of my groaning' is a heavy phrase: he hears himself. The Hebrew has 'my bone', singular, clinging to 'my flesh', and the picture is the starved man whose skin lies directly over the skeleton. The KJV has 'skin', and it is not wrong, because Radak and Meiri both explain that basar can stand for 'skin' (compare Lam 4:8 'their skin cleaves to their bones'), but the Hebrew word is 'flesh', and the Targum too has flesh. Job 19:20 uses nearly the same words. The old commentators have the groaning itself wasting the body (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David), so the sound and the shrinking are linked. Cleaving (davak) is the same verb used for a husband clinging to his wife in Gen 2:24; here it is bone that has no fat to separate it from flesh. The line is short, five words; give it room.

philological_notes.note: To cling, stick to; the word of marriage in Gen 2:24, here the bone sticking to the flesh because the fat is gone. Job 19:20 has the same phrase.
'My flesh'. KJV 'skin' is an interpretation. Radak and Meiri say the Hebrew uses 'flesh' where we would say 'skin', and cite Lam 4:8.

verses.translation_literal: I am like a desert owl of the wilderness; I have become like an owl of the ruins.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have become the desert owl, the bird of the wilderness, sitting alone in the broken places where the walls have fallen, calling out into the night.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker leaves the human world. Two birds, qa'at and kos, both on the unclean-bird list of Lev 11:17-18, both creatures of places people avoid: the midbar, the open dry country, and the chorvot, ruins, the heaps where cities used to be. No one knows exactly which birds these are. The KJV chose 'pelican' for the first, which is a water bird and which Malbim indeed reads as one, but the setting here is dry; and 'owl of the desert' for the second, where the Hebrew has 'owl of the ruins'. The KJV also renders chorvot, 'ruins', as 'desert', which loses the sense of a destroyed city. Radak and Meiri both say the cry of these birds sounds like mourning, and that is the actor's point: the man sounds like them. For an audience that knew the ruins of towns after an invasion, this is the sound of a destroyed place. 'I am like' becomes 'I have become' in the second line; the verb changes from dami (resemble) to hayiti (become), a quiet step in the speaker's slide.

philological_notes.note: An unclean bird of Lev 11:18 and Deut 14:17, of uncertain identity: pelican, cormorant or an owl. KJV 'pelican' is a tradition; 'desert owl' is a guess that fits the setting. Radak and Meiri say its voice is a mourning cry.
A second unclean bird, listed with the shalakh and yanshuf in Lev 11:17 (Rashi). The ruins (chorvot) are what is left of towns, so the owl lives where people used to.

verses.translation_literal: I lie awake, and I have become like a bird, alone, on a roof.
verses.translation_dramatic: I lie awake through the night, and I am a single bird sitting on the edge of a roof, with no mate and no flock beside it.
verses.directors_commentary: Night now. 'I lie awake' is shaqadti, the verb of the watchman who does not sleep; the same root names the almond tree, the first to wake in spring, so it is a word for being awake before everyone else. A flat roof in a Judean house is where people sleep in hot weather and talk in the evening, so the bird alone on one is an image of a lit-up courtyard emptied of company. The word tsippor is 'bird'; the KJV 'sparrow' narrows it, and the Hebrew does not say sparrow. The adjective boded is the lonely one, the 'solitary', from the root of badad, 'apart': one that has separated from the others, and in Ps 102 it is the climax of the isolation begun in verse 7. Rashi and Meiri say the bird has lost its mate. Ibn Ezra also points out that tsippor is masculine here though feminine in the Torah. Metzudat Zion offers a different sense for shaqadti, 'I hurried', and Radak 'I was diligent'; both are possible, but the context of night and solitude favours wakefulness.

philological_notes.note: To watch, stay awake; the root is shared with the almond tree, the 'waker'. Metzudat Zion takes it as 'to hurry' and Radak as 'to be diligent'; I follow the Targum, 'I was awake all night'.
A solitary bird. Rashi: a bird that sits alone without a mate. Ibn Ezra notes that tsippor is treated as masculine here.

verses.translation_literal: All the day they taunt me, my enemies; those who rave against me have sworn by me.
verses.translation_dramatic: All day long my enemies jeer at me. And those who rave at me use my name for their oaths, so that when they wish evil on themselves, they say it over mine.
verses.directors_commentary: From the night we come to the day, and from the bird to the neighbours. The verb cherfuni is 'to taunt, to reproach'; to be reproached in the ancient world was to lose honour in public, and for an exile it was worse because honour was the last possession. The second line is the difficult one. Mehollalai is a participle from the root of halal that means to act madly, to rave (as in Eccl 1:17), not 'praise'; the KJV 'they that are mad against me' preserves that. Then nishba'u bi, literally 'they have sworn by me'. The KJV and Webster have 'sworn against me', which turns it into a plot; the ASV 'do curse by me' is nearer. Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all hear a formula in which enemies swear 'may I be like this man if I am lying', so that his misery becomes a curse. Isa 65:15 shows the same usage: 'you shall leave your name for a curse to my chosen'. For actors this is the most humiliating line in the opening: he has become a byword. Ibn Ezra also reads the verse as the clue to the whole psalm, that his troubles come because he bears the enemy's scorn.

philological_notes.note: Polel participle of halal I, 'to rave, act madly', not halal 'to praise'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion connect it with holelut, 'folly', in Eccl 1:17.
'They have sworn by me': they use the speaker's fate as the form of an oath ('may I be like him'). Compare Isa 65:15 and Num 5:21. KJV 'against me' loses the formula.

verses.translation_literal: For ash like bread I have eaten, and my drinks with weeping I have mixed.
verses.translation_dramatic: For ashes have been my bread, and I have mixed my drink with weeping, until every cup is salt.
verses.directors_commentary: The two most basic acts of the day, eating and drinking, both ruined. Ash is what remained of a burnt house or an altar, and sitting in ashes was the posture of mourning (Job 2:8, Jonah 3:6); eating it is a figure, as Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David say: food tastes of ash. The Hebrew puts 'ash' first, ahead of the verb, so it lands before the bread does. Then 'my drinks': shiqquvai is plural, 'all my drinks'. The verb masakhti is the one for mixing wine with water or spices (Prov 9:2, 'she has mixed her wine'), so he does with tears what a host does with wine. The KJV 'mingled' is a good choice. The KJV puts a comma at the end of the verse and the next verse begins 'Because of thine indignation', which is correct because verse 11 is the cause. Keep the line open at its end.

philological_notes.note: Ash, the stuff of mourning (Jer 6:26, Est 4:1). Eating ash is figurative: the bread tastes like it (Metzudat David, Radak).
To mix a drink, as wine is mixed with water or spice (Prov 9:2; Metzudat Zion cites it). Rashi glosses it as 'I mingled' (mazagti).

verses.translation_literal: Because of your indignation and your wrath, for you have lifted me up and you have thrown me down.
verses.translation_dramatic: It is because of your fury and your rage. You lifted me up high, and then you flung me away.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the speaker names the cause, and it is not the enemy. Two words for anger, za'am and qetsef, sit side by side: za'am is anger that is spoken out, indignation; qetsef is the heat of wrath. Both are the king's anger, and the speaker has no doubt where the blow came from. Then the cruel image: 'you lifted me up and you threw me down.' The verb nasa is 'to lift', and hishlikh is 'to hurl, to throw away'. KJV 'lifted me up, and cast me down' is a good rendering. The ASV 'taken me up' is weaker. Rashi, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David and Malbim all read it as: God raised him so that the fall would be worse. Radak gives the image: to smash something to the ground, you first lift it high. So the lifting is not a favour; it is the wind-up. Keep a beat after 'lifted me up' before the drop.

philological_notes.note: Two near-synonyms for divine anger, 'indignation' and 'wrath'. The two roots stand together in Jer 10:10. Here they make the cause of the suffering God's own anger, not the enemy's strength.

'You lifted me and you flung me': the lifting is the wind-up for a harder fall. Rashi compares Lam 2:1 'he threw down from heaven to earth'; Radak says that to drop something hard, you must first lift it high.

verses.translation_literal: My days are like a shadow stretched out, and I, like vegetation, I wither.
verses.translation_dramatic: My days are a shadow stretched long across the ground at evening, and I am the grass that withers in the heat.
verses.directors_commentary: The first movement closes on two pictures of a day ending. The 'shadow stretched out' is the late-afternoon shadow, long and thin, about to be swallowed by the dark; Rashi says it is evening, when shadows lengthen and then are no longer seen, and Radak and Meiri cite Jer 6:4 'the shadows of the evening are stretched out'. The KJV 'a shadow that declineth' and the ASV are interpretation: the Hebrew nafuy is 'stretched out', and the sense of decline is only implied. The second line returns to the plant of verse 5. There it was lev (heart) that was struck and dried (vayyivash); here it is 'I' who wither (ivash), using the same root. The Hebrew repeats ke-'esev, 'like vegetation', exactly as in verse 5, so the speaker's heart and the whole man are now the same grass. It is the image Isaiah 40:7 will use for all flesh. The shadow is time and the grass is the body; neither can be recovered. The next verse turns to YHWH, who 'sits forever'.

philological_notes.note: 'Like a stretched-out shadow', the long shadow of late day. Rashi: evening, when shadows lengthen and vanish. Radak and Meiri compare Jer 6:4. KJV 'that declineth' interprets.
'I wither', the same root as vayyivash in verse 5. The repeated image makes the heart's drying (v. 5) the drying of the whole man.

verses.translation_literal: And you, YHWH, for ever you sit, and your remembrance [is] to a generation and a generation.
verses.translation_dramatic: But you, LORD, you remain. You are seated, and no wind of years can move you from your place. And the memory of you passes from mouth to mouth, from one generation down to the next, unbroken.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Psalm turns here, after the sufferer's long lament about vanishing like smoke and withering like grass. The opening אַתָּה, 'And you', is a hard pivot: the speaker's days are a shadow, but the one addressed does not move. Play it as a breath of relief, not as a doctrine.

The verb תֵּשֵׁב is 'you sit', and in the ancient Near East sitting is what a king does on his throne: this is enthronement language, the posture of rule. KJV's 'shalt endure' flattens the image into abstraction and turns a present state into a promise; the Hebrew has an imperfect that means a continuing state. KJV also reads זכר as 'remembrance', which is fair, but the word is the name by which a god is called on in cult (compare Exod 3:15, where 'this is my remembrance to a generation and a generation'). Repetition of 'generation, generation' is the Hebrew way of saying 'all generations' with a rolling sound, and the dramatic layer lets it roll. Rashi hears an appeal: as you endure, you must keep us, since you swore to us.

philological_notes.note: 'You sit', the verb of enthroned rule; the parallel in Ps 9:8 and 29:10 uses the same root for YHWH seated as king. KJV's 'endure' loses the throne.
'Your remembrance', the name by which YHWH is invoked and recalled in worship, as in Exod 3:15. It is not only a private memory.

verses.translation_literal: You, you will arise, you will have compassion on Zion, for [it is] time to show her favor, for the appointed time has come.
verses.translation_dramatic: You, and you alone, will rise. You will stir from your seat and turn toward Zion, toward her ruin and her silence, and you will pity her. For the hour has ripened. The time to show her favor is here, the hour that was fixed long ago has come at last.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns here on a single pronoun. After the sufferer's long fading, אַתָּה, 'you', comes first in the sentence, set against the passing days of vv. 12-13. Radak hears a man getting up from his place and rousing himself to act ("אתה כאדם שקם ממקומו ומתעורר על מעשה"): God is pictured as a king who has been seated while his city lay waste, and who now stands. Ibn Ezra reads the standing against the sitting of the previous verse.

The KJV 'Thou shalt arise' makes a plain future of what is a confident imperfect, close to a prayer. 'The time to favour her, yea, the set time' is accurate but old; 'favour' is חנן, the grace shown by a superior, and the verb 'have mercy' (רחם) is built on the same letters as the noun רֶחֶם, 'womb'. That link is my own observation: the Hebrew ear may have heard a mother's tenderness in it. Two words for time stand side by side. עֵת is the right moment; מוֹעֵד is a fixed date, the word used for the festivals, a meeting set by appointment. Radak says redemption has a measured time ("מועד וזמן קצוב"). Nothing is happening yet in the verse; it is the speaker's certainty that the date has come. Note, too, that the verse is numbered 13 in the KJV, which is why the English count runs one behind.

philological_notes.note: 'You will have compassion.' A Piel of the root that also gives רֶחֶם 'womb', so the feeling is a parent's. The link is my own reading.
An appointed time or meeting, the word used for the festivals. Set beside עֵת 'time' it makes the date fixed, not merely favourable. Radak: redemption has a fixed, measured time.

'To show her favor.' The vowel is unexpected: Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri all explain that it is the infinitive of an intensive verb with the weak nun, with the usual patah softened to a segol, as in פֶּן־אֲכֶלְךָ (Exod 33:3).

verses.translation_literal: For your servants have taken pleasure [in] her stones, and [on] her dust they show favor.
verses.translation_dramatic: For your servants love her even now: her stones, broken as they lie, and her dust, which they hold dear. They cannot look at that rubble without tenderness.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the most intimate verse of the pair. The speakers are people in exile, or in the ruined city, who love a heap of rubble. The Hebrew sets the objects before the verbs in each half (her stones, her dust), the way a person names what he loves first. In the second half the verb is reversed so the dust is raised to first position by the particle: 'and her dust, they favor it'.

KJV 'take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof' is accurate in its words, but 'favour' sounds like administrative approval. The verb is חנן, the same root as 'show favor' in the previous verse, and it carries grace and tenderness, the gesture of caressing something that belongs to you. Ibn Ezra imagines people who would kiss the dust; Radak says the same. A midrash that Rashi preserves has the exiles of Jehoiachin carrying stones and soil from Jerusalem to build a synagogue in Babylon. 'Dust' (עָפָר) is also the mourner's substance, which people throw on their heads, so it is a tender and a grieving word at once.

philological_notes.note: 'They have taken pleasure in, been pleased with'. Ibn Ezra reads it as the people's desire to see the place; the same root is used of a land that 'enjoys' its sabbaths (Lev 26:34).
'They show favor to, they treat tenderly'. It echoes לְחֶנְנָהּ in v. 14: the servants favor the dust because God is about to favor Zion.

verses.translation_literal: And nations will fear the name of YHWH, and all the kings of the earth your glory.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the nations will tremble at the Name of the LORD, and every king on earth will tremble before your glory.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera pulls back from Zion to the whole world. 'Fear' (יראה) here is awe before something that has been seen, not terror alone; the nations are the audience of the rebuilding, not its victims. The verse is built on a pair: the name of YHWH for the peoples, and your glory for the kings. Malbim hears a difference in rank. The ordinary nations, who are far away, fear the name, which is what reaches them by report; the kings, who are better placed to judge splendour, fear the glory itself, which they will see once Zion is built.

The KJV 'heathen' is the word גּוֹיִם, simply 'nations', and the English word carries a contempt the Hebrew does not have. The KJV also begins with 'So', which is a guess at the connection; the Hebrew has a plain 'and'. A subtler point: the verse switches from naming God in the third person ('the name of YHWH') to speaking to him ('your glory') in the middle of the line. The KJV keeps this but the ear does not notice; on stage the actor should turn toward God on the second half. Kings in the ancient Near East were the ones who sent embassies and tribute; their fear is political fear, a recognition that a new power is present.

philological_notes.note: 'Name' here means reputation and presence as much as a label; it is paired with כָּבוֹד (root כבד, 'weight'), 'glory'. Malbim: the name is what is heard from far off, the glory what is seen.
'Nations', the ordinary word for peoples. The KJV 'heathen' adds a religious judgement the Hebrew does not make.

verses.translation_literal: For YHWH has built Zion, he has appeared in his glory.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD has built Zion, and the stones stand where the dust lay. He has been seen in his glory.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'for' gives the reason the nations will fear: the building is done. Both verbs are perfects, 'has built' and 'has appeared', and the Psalm speaks as if the rebuilding were finished. This is the prophetic perfect, the future seen so clearly that it is told in the past tense. KJV's 'When the Lord shall build up Zion, he shall appear' turns both into a future conditional and drops the 'for', so that the verse stops explaining the previous line.

נִרְאָה is a Niphal and means 'he was seen' or 'he showed himself', the word of theophany; the claim is that God becomes visible in a city rebuilt. For a first audience that is a daring thing: in the ancient Near East, a god whose temple lay in ruins was understood to have been defeated or to have left, and the rebuilding is what proves he is back. Ibn Ezra and Radak read the line as the reason the nations will fear: they see Zion built and God visible in it.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of 'to see': 'he was seen, he appeared'. The word of theophany; the rebuilt city is where God becomes visible again.

verses.translation_literal: He has turned to the prayer of the destitute person, and he has not despised their prayer.
verses.translation_dramatic: He has turned his face toward the prayer of the stripped and the bare, the lone bush in the wasteland, and he did not hold their prayer in contempt.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse has two halves that quietly contradict each other in number. The prayer is of 'the destitute person' (singular, with the article) but the verse ends with 'their prayer' (plural). Meiri notes that the prophets shift between singular and plural in this way: one man's prayer is the people's. Ibn Ezra and Radak say this is Israel in exile, pictured as lonely, the one standing apart from the settled lands.

The word עַרְעָר is the key. The same noun occurs for a desert shrub in Jer 17:6, and Meiri and Radak cite exactly that image ("כערער בערבה", 'like a tamarisk in the wasteland'). It is used of a person only here, so the psalm is saying the sufferer is a bush alone in the dry land. Rashi gives two other roots: one who cries out, and one 'razed', from עָרוּ עָרוּ in Ps 137:7. Ibn Ezra rejects the 'razed' link as unsound. The KJV 'destitute' keeps the sense of poverty but loses the picture; 'regard' for פנה is weaker than the Hebrew, which is 'turn the face toward', as a king turns to a petitioner. The final 'not despised' is a classic understatement: the Hebrew literally says God did not treat the prayer as nothing, which was exactly what the exile's neighbours expected (Radak: "כמו שהיו חושבים בבליים").

philological_notes.note: A noun that elsewhere names a desert shrub (Jer 17:6); here it is used of a person, the destitute, bare one. Radak and Meiri read the image of a lone bush in the wasteland. Rashi offers 'one who cries out' or 'razed'; Ibn Ezra rejects the second derivation from עָרוּ עָרוּ.
'He has turned' (the face) toward; the verb is the movement of attention, and its noun פָּנִים is 'face'. The sense is of a king turning to hear a petitioner. This is my own reading.

verses.translation_literal: Let this be written for a later generation, and a people [who will be] created will praise Yah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let this be written down for the generation that comes after, so that a people not yet born, a people newly made, will lift up their voices and praise Yah.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalmist turns the scene into a document. The deliverance is to be set down in writing for those who have not yet lived. תִּכָּתֶב is a Niphal imperfect, and it can be read in two ways: as a wish, 'let it be written', or as a plain future, 'it will be written'. The packet's STEPBible rendering and the Hebrew mood both favour the wish; the KJV 'shall be written' is a fair alternative reading. Rashi hears the voice of those who see the salvation, saying that it should be recorded; Radak adds that the later generation is the one that did not see the wonders and must be told how they came about.

The real interest is the phrase עַם נִבְרָא, 'a people created'. It uses בָּרָא, the verb of Genesis 1, which is reserved for God. Rashi reads it as a new creation, a people brought from slavery to freedom, from darkness to great light; Meiri, that Israel is made new in its youth. The Targum, for its part, says the people 'who will be created', a future. The verb is Niphal participle, so 'created' without any 'shall' in the Hebrew; the KJV supplies the future but keeps 'created'. Ancient writing was not casual: a text set down was a witness for later times, and this line makes the psalm itself that witness. The divine name appears in its short form Yah, the word in the cry 'hallelu-Yah', so the verse ends on the sound of the praise it describes.

philological_notes.note: Niphal imperfect, 'let it be written' or 'it will be written'. The mood is ambiguous; the wish reading suits the prayer, the future reading the confidence of the verses before.
'Created'. The verb is the one of Gen 1:1, whose subject is God. Rashi reads a people made a new creature, out of slavery into freedom and from darkness into great light.
The short form of the divine name. It is the second half of 'hallelu-Yah', so the line ends on the sound of the praise it describes. That sound-play is my own observation.

verses.translation_literal: For he has looked down from the height of his holiness, YHWH from heaven to earth has looked.
verses.translation_dramatic: For he has bent his gaze down from the height of his holy place. From heaven to earth, the LORD has looked.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reason that the record is to be kept: God has looked down. The line is built as a staircase, from the height of his holiness, then heaven, then earth, with the divine name set in the middle like the figure on the stairs. The verb הִשְׁקִיף, 'bend over and look down', is used of someone leaning over a balcony or looking out through a window; in Deut 26:15 and Gen 18:16 it is God or the angels who look down. Meiri recalls the rabbinic saying that 'looking down' is rarely a good thing in Scripture, except in this prayer for blessing.

KJV 'the height of his sanctuary' is a fair rendering of מְרוֹם קָדְשׁוֹ, but קֹדֶשׁ is holiness rather than the building; the sanctuary here is the heavenly place. Then הִבִּיט is a different verb, a steady look, which is why YLT's 'looked attentively' catches the sense. The two verbs together are the thing the ancient audience needed to hear, a god who does not stay behind the veil of heaven. Rashi and Radak both take the object to be the affliction of his people.

philological_notes.note: 'He looked down, he leaned out to look'. The same root names a window or a lintel, so the picture is of someone leaning from a high place.
'He looked, he gazed'; a steady, attentive look. STEPBible lemma H5027.

verses.translation_literal: To hear the groaning of the prisoner, to open [up] the sons of death.
verses.translation_dramatic: He looked so that he might hear the groan of the one in chains, and open the door to those who were marked for death.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two infinitives carry the whole verse: to hear and to open. God's looking down in v. 20 has a purpose, and it is rescue. The word אֶנְקָה is a groan, the sound of someone too weak or too crushed for speech. Metzudat Zion links it to the groaning of the wounded in Ezek 26:15 ("באנוק חלל"). Ibn Ezra compares the sound to Exod 2:24, "God heard their groaning" (נַאֲקָתָם); this is a near-synonym from the related root נאק, not the same noun, but the echo is deliberate: the exile is cast as a second Egypt, and the prisoner's cry is the cry of the slaves.

The KJV 'those that are appointed to death' paraphrases בְּנֵי תְמוּתָה, literally 'sons of death'. The Hebrew idiom is common: 'sons of' marks what a person belongs to. Rashi glosses תְּמוּתָה as one sick to die; Ibn Ezra, as those prepared for slaughter; Radak and Meiri, as people near to death from their distress. Metzudat David takes לְפַתֵּחַ as loosening the bonds of those led off to die; Metzudat Zion compares Job 12:18. The verb is literally 'to open', and a prison was a place to be opened. Nothing in the text says the prisoners were condemned by a court; the picture is of captivity so harsh that death is the expected end.

philological_notes.note: 'The groaning of.' A groan or sigh of distress (lemma אֲנָקָה). Ibn Ezra compares Exod 2:24, נַאֲקָתָם, which is from the related root נאק and not the same noun; Metzudat Zion compares Ezek 26:15 for the sense of the groan of the wounded.
'Sons of death.' The idiom marks those who belong to death. Rashi: one who is sick unto death. Ibn Ezra: those made ready for slaughter, with the same ending as תְּקוּמָה and תְּרוּמָה.

verses.translation_literal: To recount in Zion the name of YHWH, and his praise in Jerusalem.
verses.translation_dramatic: So that they may tell it in Zion, the name of the LORD, and sing his praise in Jerusalem.
verses.directors_commentary:
The freed prisoners now become tellers. The infinitive לְסַפֵּר, 'to recount', is the verb of a witness telling a story in order, from the root that also gives 'book' and 'number'. Ibn Ezra's one-line comment is 'now is the time of salvation'. The setting is the city itself: Zion and Jerusalem are used as a pair, a normal Hebrew parallelism, and not two places.

KJV's 'To declare' is a fair rendering, but the verb is not 'declare' in the sense of proclaiming; it is to give an account, to narrate. A modern reader should imagine pilgrims in the courtyard of the Temple telling what happened to them. 'His praise' (תְּהִלָּה) is the noun that gives the book of Psalms its Hebrew title, Tehillim, so the Psalm is describing its own business. Radak notes that the verse doubles the previous idea in different words, a parallelism that was heard, not read.

philological_notes.note: 'To recount, to tell in order'. The same root gives 'scribe', 'book' and 'number', so it is telling that can be counted and recorded.
'His praise'; the noun from which the Hebrew name of the whole book, Tehillim, comes.

verses.translation_literal: In [the] gathering of peoples together, and kingdoms, to serve YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: When the peoples are gathered together, and the kingdoms with them, to serve the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The prisoners' story fills the courtyard, and the audience grows: whole peoples and kingdoms come in. The verse has no main verb of its own; it is a time clause hanging from the one before, which gives it a breathless, unfinished quality that actors should keep. The Hebrew begins with an infinitive, בְּהִקָּבֵץ, 'in the being-gathered', a passive: they are gathered, and the one who gathers is not named.

The key word is לַעֲבֹד, 'to serve', and it is the same verb used for a slave's labor and for a subject's service to a king. KJV's 'serve' is right; BBE's 'give worship' is softer. This is the political side of the vision: the kingdoms (מַמְלָכוֹת) who once ruled over the exiles now come to serve the God of the exiles. Ibn Ezra compares Zeph 3:9, 'to serve him with one shoulder' (שְׁכֶם אֶחָד). 'Together' (יַחְדָּו) is a poetic form that stresses unity.

philological_notes.note: 'To serve', the verb of a servant to a master and of cultic service. Here peoples and kingdoms take the posture of servants (עֲבָדֶיךָ, v. 15). Ibn Ezra compares Zeph 3:9.

verses.translation_literal: He has afflicted my strength in the way; he has cut short my days.
verses.translation_dramatic: On the road he wore me down. My strength is spent, and my days have been cut off short.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice of the lone sufferer returns after the vision of the nations, and the mood drops from the great future to a single worn body on a road. The verse does not name who did this. Rashi sees it as a return to the first complaint, and supplies the subject: 'my enemy afflicted my strength on the way', joined to the lament of vv. 11-12, 'you have lifted me up and thrown me down; my days are like a lengthening shadow'. Radak and Meiri also read the enemy, and Radak describes the exile's march from place to place under hard masters, which wears the strength and shortens life. Ibn Ezra says the road itself shortens life, and that those who come in exile may die on the way before they reach Jerusalem. The alternative is that the subject is God, which follows the parallel with v. 11, where it is explicitly 'you' who threw the speaker down. That second reading is mine and not Rashi's; the Hebrew leaves it open.

The KJV 'weakened' for עִנָּה is soft. The verb is the one for 'afflict' or 'humble', used for the oppression of the Hebrews in Egypt, and it means to bring low by force. 'In the way' is the Hebrew בַּדֶּרֶךְ with the article: the road, the journey itself, the one that was walked. 'Cut short' is קִצַּר, to shorten like a rope or a life, a physical word.

philological_notes.note: 'He has afflicted, brought low.' The same verb that is used for the oppression of Israel in Egypt. The subject is unstated; Rashi supplies 'my enemy' ("אוֹיְבִי").
'My strength.' The packet marks a Ketiv/Qere here and the gloss follows the Qere; the sense is the same either way.
'He has cut short.' A physical verb, as of a rope or a harvest being cut short.

verses.translation_literal: I say, my God, do not lift me up in the half of my days; in a generation of generations [are] your years.
verses.translation_dramatic: I say it, and I say it low, as a man says it who has nothing left to bargain with: My God, do not take me up now. Do not lift me out of my days when I have lived only half of them. You are the One whose years run on from age to age to age, and mine are so few.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker is a man who feels himself being cut off in mid-life. The verb 'lift up' (תַעֲלֵנִי) is the verb for hauling something up and away: it is the word used for taking a sheaf up from a field or for lifting a person out of a pit, and here it means being removed from the land of the living. KJV's 'take me not away' is a fair paraphrase but loses the physical image of being picked up and carried off. The tense matters too: the Hebrew 'I say' is an imperfect, an ongoing, repeated prayer, and KJV's 'I said' turns it into a story told afterwards. Play it as something muttered over and over in the night.

The argument is a contrast of scale. 'The half of my days' is the middle of a normal lifespan, which in the ancient world might be only a few decades and which Ps 90 sets at seventy or eighty. Against it stands the unusual 'generation of generations' (דוֹר דּוֹרִים), a doubled word that has no plural-of-plural in English; KJV's 'throughout all generations' flattens it into a prepositional phrase. The speaker does not demand anything; he sets his short span next to God's endless one and lets the gap make the plea. Rashi and Radak hear the 'I' as the whole people, and Metzudat David as every generation, but the singular voice is what the actor should carry.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of 'to go up': 'do not make me go up', that is, do not lift me away. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'removal', as in the sheaf that is taken up in its season (Job 5:26).
'In a generation of generations': a construct chain that repeats the root to give an unbroken series. The preposition is 'in', so the years of God are located within the whole sequence of ages.
'In the half of my days': the middle of one's span, a life broken off before its measure is full.

verses.translation_literal: To the face [of time] you founded the earth, and the work of your hands [are] the heavens.
verses.translation_dramatic: Before the first morning, you laid the earth's foundations, stone by stone in the dark. And the heavens, that great arch over every head, are the work of your hands.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice turns from the dying man to the one who made everything he stands on. 'Founded' (יָסַד) is a builder's word, used of laying the footings of a house or of the Temple, so the earth is pictured as a building and the heavens as its roof; Malbim spells that image out. The word לְפָנִים is the interesting one: it is literally 'to the faces', and it means 'formerly, of old, at the front of time'. Rashi glosses it simply as 'at the beginning'. KJV's 'of old' is correct but archaic, and 'laid the foundation' in an archaic voice makes this sound like a hymn for the pew rather than a boast made to a God who is about to be asked to spare a life.

There is a quiet polemic too. In the surrounding cultures, heaven and earth were themselves divine, or were split from the body of a slain god, as in the Babylonian Enuma Elish. Here they are 'the work of your hands', made things, and so they can wear out, which is what the next verse says. Ibn Ezra and Radak hear in it a denial that the world is eternal. The sentence order puts 'the work of your hands' before 'the heavens': the maker's hands come first in the line, the sky last.

philological_notes.note: 'Formerly, of old': a plural of 'face' used as an adverb of time, like 'in front of', here the front of history. Rashi: 'from the beginning'; Metzudat Zion compares Ruth 4:7.
'You founded': the builder's verb for laying the foundation of a building. Malbim develops the picture of the earth as the foundation and the heavens as the roof of the world's house.
'Work of your hands': craftsmanship. The heavens are not a god but an artefact, and so subject to wear.

token_glosses.gloss: to the face of time, of old

verses.translation_literal: They, they will perish, and you, you will stand; and all of them like the garment will wear out, like the clothing you will change them, and they will be changed.
verses.translation_dramatic: They will perish, these heavens and this earth. But you will stand. Every one of them will wear thin as a garment wears, and like a robe you will fold them away and put on another, and they will pass, and be changed.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm: the sky and the ground, the most stable things a person knows, are set against the one who stands. The two pronouns are stressed in the Hebrew: 'they' and 'you' are placed at the head of their clauses, so the verse is built as a sharp contrast, 'they will perish, but you, you will stand'. KJV's 'wax old' is the archaizing choice for בלה, a word for cloth worn out, falling to pieces, and it is plain wear, not poetry. The image is a household one: a woman's or a servant's work of looking after clothes. A garment is worn until it thins, then it is taken off and replaced.

The last two verbs carry a wordplay KJV obscures: 'you change them' (תַּחֲלִיפֵם) and 'they are changed' (יַחֲלֹפוּ) are the same root חלף. God exchanges, and the thing exchanged passes on; the English 'changed' twice catches the echo, though 'pass' also lies in the root. The Hebrew says nothing about a new heaven here, as Metzudat David reads it with Isa 65; it says only that they will be swapped like clothes. Rabbinic readers disagree about whether this is destruction or renewal (Radak mentions philosophers who held the world would end; Ibn Ezra reads it as the particulars perishing while the laws remain), so do not play it as the end of the world but as a change of outfit, done calmly, by someone who is not troubled by it.

philological_notes.note: 'They will perish, be lost': the verb for what is lost or destroyed. Here it is the heavens and earth that go, a claim that the world is not eternal.

The same root twice: Hiphil 'you cause them to pass/exchange them' and Qal 'they pass on'. Rashi: like a man who turns his clothing and takes it off. Radak: God changes them or replaces them with others as he wills.
'They wear out': of cloth that frays and rots. Metzudat Zion links it to rotting and wasting, as in the leaf that does not wither (Ps 1:3).

verses.translation_literal: And you [are] he, and your years will not be finished.
verses.translation_dramatic: But you are he. You are the same. And your years will never be counted out.
verses.directors_commentary:
The shortest verse of the section is the one the others lean on. 'You are he' (אַתָּה־הוּא) is easy to miss: KJV's 'thou art the same' is a good sense, but the Hebrew is bare and almost a name: the pronoun 'he' stands as predicate with no noun. It is close to the 'I am he' of Deut 32:39 and Isaiah 41:4 and 43:10, where God says it of himself, and in the English translations that also reads like an echo of the divine name. Rashi takes it as 'the one who stands and endures', Metzudat David as 'the thing that remains in its being'. Say it flat, without a flourish, after the long contrast of the last verse.

The second half is a measure of time. 'Your years' (שְׁנוֹתֶיךָ) answers 'my days' (v.25): his days are numbered and halved, God's years do not 'come to completion' (יִתַּמּוּ, from תמם, to be complete). KJV's 'have no end' is a fair sense, but the verb is about running out like a sum that is finished. The same verse is quoted in Hebrews 1:10-12, in the Greek version, of the Son.

philological_notes.note: 'You are he': the predicate pronoun alone, the same form as the declaration 'I am he' elsewhere in Scripture. The sense is unchanging being: Rashi 'the one who stands and endures'; Ibn Ezra 'he in truth, and there is none but you'.
'They will be finished, completed': from תם, completeness, so the years are never rounded off to a sum. Metzudat Zion: from 'completion and fulfillment'.

verses.translation_literal: The sons of your servants will dwell, and their seed will be established before you.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the children of your servants will have a home. They will dwell, and their offspring will stand firm in your sight.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on a promise for the next generation, which is what the first half-lived man can still hope for. 'Servants' (עֲבָדִים) is not a slave class here but the title of those who belong to the king: the court term for loyal attendants, and in the Psalms a name for the faithful. The sons of such servants are the ones who inherit their place. The verb 'dwell' (יִשְׁכּוֹנוּ) is the verb of settling in a tent or a land, so it is not 'continue' as KJV puts it, which turns a picture of a home into an abstraction; BBE's 'safe resting-place' goes the other way and adds the safety. Radak hears it as dwelling in the land after the return, Meiri as living there in security.

The last verb 'be established' (יִכּוֹן, from כון) is something set firm and fixed in place, as a throne or a house is. 'Before you' (לְפָנֶיךָ) echoes the 'of old' (לְפָנִים) in v.26: the same word for 'face', first of time, now of the face of God. The seed that stands 'before your face' is under God's eye, and Radak takes it to mean serving him for ever. Because the verb is singular, the 'seed' is a collective that acts as one.

philological_notes.note: 'They will dwell': the verb for settling and living in a place, as in a tent or a land. Radak and Meiri take it as dwelling in their land; Metzudat David names Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
Niphal of כון: 'be set firm, be established', singular because the 'seed' is a collective. Metzudat Zion links it to 'preparation'.
